Prayopavesha: the Fast Unto Death

Stories from the Ramayana

Prayopavesha: the Fast Unto Death

When a Month Had Passed, and the Party Saw No Way Forward

Everyday telling — Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 53–55

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read it slowly, as if you were sitting at home among everyone, telling it to them.

This book is a difficult story. In it the vanaras sit down in defeat — and resolve to fast unto death. Where despair comes, read slowly and heavily; where Hanuman reasons with them, bring patience and firmness into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Angada worried and firm, Tara slow and persuasive, Hanuman humble and firm, Jambavan calm.

(The purple cues) tell you when to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak.

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 53–55 — prayopavesha, the resolve to fast unto death. The cave story of the party that went south is in the book before this one. Anything else you may want to know about the story is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Angada — son of Vali and Tara, the young vanara prince, now the crown prince. Leader of the party that goes south. In this book he is the one who puts the hardest proposal before the party.

Hanuman — Sugriva's minister, son of Vayu the wind. A powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, a long tail, a gentle and devoted face, a saffron dhoti. He is the one who speaks for effort against despair.

Jambavan — the aged king of the bears, son of Brahma. Wise and patient — the party's eldest counsellor.

Tara — a senior and respected vanara of the party (this is not Tara, Vali's wife — this is an elderly vanara named Tara). He suggests a different way out.

Nila — son of Agni, commander of the vanara army. He is in the party that goes south.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras. Warm brown fur, a long tail, royal dress, a plain gold crown. He gave the party one month — and he is held to be harsh by nature.

Rama — prince of Ayodhya. He does not appear in person in this book — but Angada says it was Rama himself who consecrated him as crown prince.

1 · On the Seashore · · ON THE SEASHORE

Swayamprabha had brought the vanaras out of the cave — and they stood on the shore of the sea. Behind them lay the Vindhya mountain, beside them the Prasravana mountain — and before them Mahodadhi, the vast southern ocean.

The vanaras looked at the sea — and they did not understand what had happened. They had gone into the cave to look for water — and now they stood on the shore of the sea.

And then it struck them — (slowly, in a wondering voice) a month had passed.

They had set out in the month of Ashvayuja — on Sugriva's command, in search of Sita. And now that month was over — and Sita had not been found.

Angada looked at the elderly vanaras — Jambavan, Tara, Nila — and at all the vanaras of the party. On every face was the same question — What do we do now?

Angada said in a gentle voice — “Brothers, sit down. I have something to say.”

The vanaras sat down on the shore of the sea — and Angada stood up to speak.

Pause and think — A month had passed — and the vanaras had not even noticed. Does time sometimes slip away like that — without telling us? And when the time is gone and the work is not done, what should one do — go back, or stop and think?

2 · Angada's Proposal · · ANGADA'S PROPOSAL

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it holds the resolve to fast unto death.

Angada said —

Angada said: “We all set out on Sugriva's command — in the month of Ashvayuja. We were given one month. That month has passed — and we have not found Sita.”

“Sugriva is harsh by nature — and as a king he will not forgive offenders. If we go back, he will count us offenders — and give us the punishment of death.”

“So, brothers, this is what is right now — let us sit here and do prayopavesha — the fast unto death. Give up food and water, and sit here on the shore of the sea. Bid farewell in our minds to our homes, our families and our wealth.”

“Better to die here than to go back and die. At least here we sit by our own choice — there we would be punished.”

The vanaras said nothing. No one spoke — because there was truth in what Angada said. The month had passed — and Sugriva's command had been broken.

Pause and think — Angada said — better to die here than to go back and die. Is that defeat — or a resolve taken by one's own mind? And when someone says “there is no way left”, is there truly no way — or can we simply not see the way?

3 · Tara's Other Way · · TARA'S OTHER WAY

Then Tara, the senior vanara of the party, spoke — he was elderly, respected, and everyone listened to him.

Tara said: “Why die? Come, let us go back into that cave — the one we have just come out of. There are golden trees there, lakes of golden lotuses, fruits and roots, drinks — there we can live happily.”

“Neither Sugriva nor Indra can come there — no one can find us there. We will live there — and no one will punish us.”

Some vanaras liked this — because the cave had everything. There was food, there was water, there was gold — and there was no fear.

But Hanuman watched in silence. He respected Tara — moon-faced, good at heart. But this way? No — this way was not right.

Hanuman knew — Angada was brave, wise, a worthy heir to Vali and Sugriva. If Angada chose this way, he would leave his dharma behind — and the search for Sita would be left behind too.

Pause and think — Tara said — let us go back to the cave, there is everything there. Is living happily the greatest goal — or is finishing the work? And when someone suggests a way that sounds good, should we take it at once — or think first?

4 · Hanuman Takes Angada Aside · · HANUMAN TAKES ANGADA ASIDE

Hanuman saw it — Angada was listening to Tara, and his mind was wavering. Hanuman thought — Angada must be saved — from this wrong way.

Hanuman called Angada aside — not before everyone, but alone. He knew — it is not good to reason with someone before everyone; words spoken alone sink into the heart.

Hanuman said: “Prince, you are more capable than your father Vali — in battle, and in holding a kingdom. As your father held the vanara kingdom firmly, so can you.”

Hanuman praised Angada — his courage, his wisdom, his inheritance. He reminded Angada of who he was, and what was expected of him.

And he gently explained — taking Tara's advice would not be right. Hiding in the cave — that is not the work of a vanara prince. That is running away from one's dharma.

Hanuman also said — “Nothing comes from despair. Effort is the way — the one who strives is the one who finds the fruit.”

Pause and think — Hanuman reasoned with Angada alone, not before everyone. When you must reason with someone, is it better to speak alone — or before everyone? And Hanuman first praised Angada — and then advised him. Does praise open the heart?

5 · Angada's Resolve · · ANGADA'S RESOLVE

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it holds the resolve to fast unto death.

Angada heard Hanuman's humble and righteous words — but his mind did not change.

Angada said: “Hanuman, your words are right — but my resolve is also right. My effort has failed — my counsels are divided — I am powerless. How can I live in Kishkindha after going back, like an orphan, like a weakling?”

“Sugriva did not consecrate me as crown prince — it was Rama, the king of men, who consecrated me, he who does the hardest deeds with ease. Sugriva was never pleased with me — and now he will have his chance to destroy me.”

“Better than imprisonment and suffering is prayopavesha. Permit me, all of you — and go back to your homes. I swear — I will not return to the city. I will fast here only — death alone is best for me.”

Angada saluted the elderly vanaras — and tears came to his eyes. Then he spread the darbha grass — and sat down.

He sat — calm, firm, and unmoving in his resolve.

Pause and think — Angada said — Rama made me crown prince, not Sugriva. Was this already in Angada's mind — that Sugriva was not pleased with him? And when someone says “this is what I will do”, should we stop them — or hear them out?

6 · All Sit Down Together · · ALL SIT DOWN TOGETHER

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it holds the resolve to fast unto death.

The vanaras looked at Angada — seated on the darbha grass, on the shore of the sea. And they too made their resolve.

They all sat down around Angada — blaming Sugriva, and praising Vali. They said — “We will sit here too — we will fast unto death too.”

No one spoke — no one moved. The waves of the sea came and went — and the vanaras sat on.

Jambavan sat too — calm, elderly, and worried. Hanuman sat too — but in his mind was only one thought — there is still a way. Effort is the way.

Night fell — and the vanaras sat on. On the shore of the sea, beneath the stars, in the moonlight — all was quiet.

And here this story pauses — on the shore of the sea, with a resolve, and with a question — is there truly no way left?

Pause and think — All the vanaras sat down with Angada. Is sitting together also a kind of friendship — “you are not alone”? And Hanuman sat — but in his mind was the thought of effort. Can effort go on in the mind even while sitting still?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this book the vanaras sat down on the shore of the sea — because a month had passed, and Sita had not been found. Angada proposed the fast unto death — Tara suggested going back to the cave — and Hanuman took Angada aside and reasoned with him.

Angada did not change his resolve — and all the vanaras sat down with him. But in Hanuman's mind was one thought — effort is the way.

Ask the listeners:

1. A month had passed — and the vanaras had not even noticed. Does time sometimes slip away like that?

2. Angada said — better to die here than to go back and die. Is that defeat — or a resolve taken by one's own mind?

3. Tara said — let us go back to the cave, there is everything there. Is living happily the greatest goal?

4. Hanuman reasoned with Angada alone — when you must reason with someone, is it better to speak alone?

5. All the vanaras sat down with Angada — is sitting together also a kind of friendship?

6. In Hanuman's mind was the thought of effort — can effort go on in the mind even while sitting still?

7. Was there truly no way left — or was the way about to appear?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 53–55 — prayopavesha, the resolve to fast unto death.

On the seashore — sarga 53

Swayamprabha leaving the vanaras on the shore of the sea; the month having passed; the setting out in the month of Ashvayuja and the ending of the time limit — this is in sarga 53.

Angada's proposal — sarga 53

Angada speaking in a gentle voice to the elderly vanaras — Sugriva is harsh by nature and will not forgive offenders; better to fast unto death here than to go back and face the punishment of death; bidding farewell in the mind to home, family and wealth — this is in sarga 53.

Consecrated by Rama — sarga 53

Angada's words — “Sugriva did not consecrate me as crown prince — Rama, the king of men, consecrated me” — this is in sarga 53.

Tara's other way — sarga 54

The senior vanara Tara's suggestion — go back to the cave, where there are fruits, roots, drinks and gold, where we can live happily, where neither Sugriva nor Indra can come — this is in sarga 54. Here Tara is a vanara — not Tara, Vali's wife.

Hanuman takes Angada aside — sarga 54

Hanuman reasoning with Angada alone; the stratagem of bheda — praising Angada that he is more capable than his father Vali and can hold the vanara kingdom firmly; warning him against Tara's counsel — this is in sarga 54.

Angada's resolve — sarga 55

Angada hearing Hanuman's words yet not changing his resolve — better fasting unto death than imprisonment and suffering; permitting all to go home; the vow “I will not return to the city, I will fast here only”; saluting the elders, tears, spreading darbha grass and sitting down — this is in sarga 55.

All sit down together — sarga 55

All the vanaras sitting down around Angada; blaming Sugriva and praising Vali while resolving to fast unto death — this is in sarga 55.

What happens next

The vanaras sit on the seashore on their fast — and here this book pauses. Their fast is broken by the coming of Sampati — Sampati's story is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of prayopavesha pauses — on the shore of the sea, with a resolve, and with a question — is there truly no way left?

And whenever it feels to you that time has passed and no way can be seen, remember Hanuman — in whose mind, even sitting still, there was only one thought — effort is the way.

— The End —
